newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Socialists show little sign of compromise.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialists show little sign of compromise.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists showed little sign of giving way on Tuesday to demands for early elections fuelled by deep economic crisis, despite fresh street protests and threats of nationwide strikes.

Pressure mounted on the government from its own people and international lenders. The outgoing president, an opposition supporter, warned Bulgaria risked becoming a dismal example of how to bungle the transition from communism.
"Bulgaria is the first post-communist state that has failed in the transition to a market economy and is about to fail in the transition to democracy," Zhelyu Zhelev told the Continent daily.

After hinting at compromise on Monday, the embattled Socialists announced on Tuesday they were willing to hold talks with the opposition on elections but would propose forming a new government with a policy programme for 500 days.

The opposition said it still wanted parliament to pass its "salvation declaration", the issue which sparked a violent siege of the legislature on Friday, and insisted a general election must be held soon.

Zhelev has declined to invite the Socialists' prime minister-designate Nikolai Dobrev to form a new cabinet to replace the Socialist government of Zhan Videnov, who resigned as prime minister on December 21.
Asked how long the new government should remain in office, Mariela Miteva, a member of the Socialist leadership, said:

"The question is not the term, but the situation." Emergency laws for economic stabilisation had to be approved before elections, and polls could only be held "in conditions of civil peace", she told reporters.

The opposition walked out of parliament on Friday after the ex-communist Socialists refused to vote on their "salvation declaration", which calls for early elections and negotations with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank on an economic programme to be conducted by an all-party team.
At least 196 people were hurt in clashes soon after between protesters and police.

Miteva said the Socialists would attend Sunday's parliamentary session at which opposition president-elect Petar Stoyanov will be sworn in. Stoyanov said he had agreed to meet Socialist leaders, probably on Wednesday.
Leaders of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) met on Tuesday and said later they opposed the formation of a new long-term cabinet from the present parliamentary majority.
The quick formation of a new cabinet is seen as vital to secure a new funding agreement with the IMF and avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.
The World Bank said on Tuesday it was extremely worried about Bulgaria's economy and urged the implementation of a stalled programme of privatisation and other reforms.

Annual inflation for 1996 was 310.8 percent. The Socialists' critics blame the party's powerful business allies for capital flight which has helped push the lev down to nearly 700 to the dollar from 70 a year ago.
Some 20,000 people marched in Sofia on Tuesday in what has become a daily ritual similar to the long-running anti-government rallies in neighbouring Serbia.
"We shall insist on early general elections as this is the only realistic way to get out of the crisis, but the Socialists are trying to bargain," UDF leader Ivan Kostov told the crowd.

The Sofia theatre said it planned to put on a free play performance for opposition supporters. International tennis player Katerina Maleeva told the rally that although she herself was not poor she wanted a free and democratic society.

At least 6,000 students earlier marched the five km (three miles) from the student housing district to the city centre carrying blue UDF flags, Bulgarian national flags and one black banner reading "They buried Bulgaria".
"We will be in the streets every day until they give up power and admit their guilt over the awful economic crisis in this country," said Sofia University student Violeta Ivanova.
The main opposition trade union Podkrepa said nationwide one-hour warning strikes would start from Wednesday.
"The nationwide strike will begin tomorrow with one-hour effective protests," Podkrepa leader Konstantin Trenchev said. Under Bulgarian law, full strikes require a week's notice.
Videnov's government, elected in December 1994, is half-way through its mandate.
